description: We’re Lisa and Boris, with backgrounds in aerospace engineering, geoinformatics, and computational mechanics. Our interests include planetary exploration, remote sensing, and turning scientific data into useful, interactive tools.
summary:
If a solar array is damaged during a mission to the Moon’s south pole, astronauts may need to find an alternate landing site or a place where the remaining panels can spend more time in sunlight. If the primary antenna is damaged, they need to know where and when a direct link to Earth may be possible and which direction to point a backup antenna. An onboard version of AstroClark could help the crew assess these options immediately using preloaded data, even without a live link to mission control.

Before launch, mission planners can use the AstroClark prototype to compare landing sites, dates, and surface-stay durations and identify backup options. Built for NASA’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, its interactive map uses NASA terrain and orbital data to rank candidate sites by slope, expected sunlight exposure, and potential direct-to-Earth contact windows with NASA’s Deep Space Network.
details:
AstroClark is an interactive lunar south pole landing-site navigator. Before launch, mission planners can compare candidate sites, touchdown times, and surface-stay durations to identify backup options. During a mission, an onboard version with preloaded data could help astronauts act without a live link to mission control. If a solar array is damaged, the crew could look for a sunnier alternate landing site or a better place to deploy the remaining panels. If the primary antenna is damaged, they could check where and when a backup antenna might have a clear path to Earth and which direction to point it.

How it works. AstroClark uses NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data to calculate the terrain skyline at each sampled location, accounting for lunar curvature and height above the ground. NASA/JPL SPICE data provide the positions needed to track the Sun and individual Deep Space Network (DSN) dishes. The tool checks those directions against the local skyline and applies each dish’s published operating limits to estimate potential two-way contact windows. Its ranking combines terrain slope, sunlight, and contact time, and rewards locations with strong neighboring options.

How to use it. Enter a touchdown date and time in UTC and a stay duration in hours. In Scoring criteria, adjust solar-panel and antenna heights, minimum sunlight and contact percentages, maximum slope, and the weight of each criterion. The map shows color-coded scores and flags excluded or uncertain points. Select a region to inspect its slope, sunlight, and contact results, or choose Compare landing sites to view two regions side by side. Select a DSN dish and move the mission-time slider to see when the Sun or the line of sight to that dish clears the terrain. Open AstroClark

How we built and verified it. Our team selected and documented the authoritative data and published methods behind the calculations, designed the algorithm, set the adjustable screening criteria, and verified the results, including spot-checks against JPL Horizons. We used Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, and Rasterio for data preparation, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the web prototype, hosted on ChatGPT Sites. AI tools, including Codex, helped implement our technical specifications in code and refine the interface and visual design.

GIT: https://github.com/Lisa4-dot/astroClark
